### Summary of the comparison results (generated by this run)

#### Data and scope

We analyze 1,008 market-hour keys from seven first-of-month days in June–December 2019. Of these, 807 satisfy the 48-of-60 trade-minute rule. The six markets combine Bitfinex, Bitstamp and Coinbase with BTC/USD and ETH/USD. These independent Tardis recordings are not the authors' original data. Only 1 June is inside the period of the supplied March 2020 SSRN preprint. FAST_MODE recomputes transaction proxies from minute bars and loads the precomputed benchmarks of Section 5; it does not reconstruct ES, PI or CRT25 from raw trades and books.

#### Main comparisons

For BTC, mean within-venue Pearson correlations of AR are 0.752 with QS, 0.802 with ES and 0.685 with CRT25. AR ranks first for these three targets. For PI, dollar volume has a higher correlation (0.604) than AR (0.577). Mean correlations give each venue equal weight. The ETH mean includes Bitstamp ETH with only 28 eligible hours, so market-specific counts remain important.

After controlling for ranked hourly volatility, AR's partial Spearman correlations on the five larger samples range from 0.408 to 0.611 for QS, 0.514 to 0.671 for ES, and 0.223 to 0.470 for CRT25. The positive association of trading activity with costs generally weakens or reverses after this control. This supports a role for shared volatility but does not identify a causal mechanism. The conclusion does not extend uniformly to PI: most AR–PI partial correlations are near zero, and Bitstamp BTC is negative. Bitstamp ETH is reported separately because its sample is small.

The date-block bootstrap uses 999 common date draws across markets, reranking observations in every draw. Its individual 95% percentile intervals are preliminary: there are only seven selected dates and no multiple-comparison correction. Undefined bootstrap coefficients are excluded and counted. These intervals do not remove the selection limitations of first-of-month observations.

In BTC volatility terciles, AR has the highest mean correlation with QS and ES in both low and high regimes. For CRT25 in the high-volatility regime, CS and AR are nearly equal. PI has different leaders. Return and volume splits are also retained in the full tables. These are descriptive splits of the whole sample, not holdout thresholds.

#### Levels and venue ordering

Correlation performance differs from level accuracy. AR can track changes while overstating small spreads. For Bitfinex BTC against QS, full-sample MAE for scaled Amihud is 0.724 bp, almost equal to the zero baseline (0.725 bp). A small raw error alone therefore does not establish useful cost measurement. Amihud and Kyle are multiplied by 10,000 following the comparison convention; this does not remove their different dimensions or Kyle's dependence on volume units.

AR exactly reproduces the QS ordering of all three venues in 75.9% of 158 BTC hours and 61.5% of 26 ETH hours. TX and volume are reversed by liquidity orientation. Tied rankings are excluded and denominators are reported. The 16.7% uniform-permutation reference is not a significance test and does not account for persistent venue ordering.

#### Temporal diagnostic

We fit the same one-proxy affine regression separately for each target and market on June–October, then evaluate on November–December. Training means, standard deviations, regression coefficients and median baselines use training hours only. QS, absolute ES and CRT25 predictions are clipped at zero by one fixed rule; PI remains signed. All eight calibrated models and unsuccessful results are retained. The test does not select a winning model.

Calibrated AR improves test MAE over the training median on 4 of five larger-sample markets for QS and 4 of five for ES. Coinbase BTC is an exception: MAE skill is -27.8% for QS and -28.1% for ES. Bitstamp ETH has only one test hour and is omitted from the main chart. Only two selected test dates are available, so no precise confidence interval for transfer quality is claimed. Per-date errors are saved. This is a test of contemporaneous cost measurement on later dates, not a forecast of next-hour costs.

#### Sensitivity and definitions

Changing the maximum quote age from 60 to 30 seconds changes partial correlations by at most 0.0244. This leaves the ten-second grid frequency unchanged. The 25-level book fills the target on both sides in 99.851% of recorded valid book snapshots, weighted by snapshot counts across all recorded hours. Insufficient-depth snapshots are excluded, not extrapolated; CRT25 remains different from a 50-level reconstruction.

Absolute ES is the main definition, while signed ES is retained as a sensitivity check (Section 5). Negative ES minima in the supplied preprint's tables are incompatible with its printed absolute-value formula. PI uses signed midpoint changes, and QS preserves the mean-of-minute-means averaging of Section 3. Definitions are documented rather than tuned to match the authors' values.

#### Overfitting considerations and further work

The core comparison contains 8 proxies × 4 targets × 6 markets. Reporting only favorable cells could overstate performance. We preserve all comparisons, keep one calibration specification, use a temporal split, compare with zero and training-median baselines, and report date-block uncertainty. A fixed seed ensures repeatability, not protection against overfitting. No multiple-testing adjustment is applied, and neither the tiny ETH sample nor the two test dates supports a broad generalization claim. Quantile dependence and the principal-component composite are omitted from this study; this is a scope reduction, not evidence that those methods are unhelpful.

Longer independent samples, more test dates and investigation of quote-grid timing would be useful extensions.

Language-model assistance was used to implement and review code and to draft explanations. All numbers above are computed in this run from the real-data tables; the artificial examples in Sections 4 and 5 are explicitly labelled checks.
